title: Held in the heart
hookLine: I have held the Name in my heart; nothing equals it (Salok M9 57, ang 1429)
tomorrow: Saloks at the close of a reading
last: RAHIO — STILL THERE WHEN IT'S CLEARED.

lines: WHAT HE CHOSE TO SAY LAST.
cards: Last words get remembered. An aunt's final sentence gets repeated at family gatherings for years. A letter's last line is the one people copy out and keep in a wallet.
Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks come near the very end of the Guru Granth Sahib, and the fifty-seventh, his last, sits close to the final page.
After all the saloks about passing, about chains, about friends who leave, what does he choose to say last? Not a warning. Not a complaint.
A plain statement of what he's holding on to.

teach.b: Salok fifty-seven, Ang fourteen twenty-nine. Raam naam ur mai gahio: I have grasped the Name of the Lord in my heart. Ur is the heart, the chest, the place you'd press a hand to.
Gahio is a grip word: seized, held tight, the way a climber holds a rope.

teach.h: SAM NAHEE KOI: NOTHING EQUALS IT.
teach.b: Then: jaa kai sam nahee koi. Sam means equal. There is nothing equal to it.
Raam here, as across Gurbani, is a name for the one God who pervades everything, not only the hero of the Ramayana.
The second line, in paraphrase: remembering it, every trouble is erased, and the sight of You is granted. Sankat is a crisis, a tight spot. Daras is the sight of the beloved, the glimpse of God.
Look at how the collection has moved. It started with the world as a dream and a wall of sand. It went through strength gone, chains, friends gone.
Then the turn: the Name remains.

teach.h: FROM A DREAM TO I HAVE HELD IT.
teach.b: And now the last word is personal: I have held it.
Not the Name exists somewhere, but it is in my heart, gripped tight. Sikh tradition hears the whole set as the Guru's testimony near his martyrdom in Delhi, and this as its final line.
Heard that way, this is a man about to lose everything the world can take, saying that the one thing he held couldn't be taken. Whatever the date of composition, that is how the tradition hears it.

how: Salok fifty-seven is the last of Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks and is read near the very end of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib.

o: the mind, where worries keep turning
the heart, where the Name is held tight
the hand, which grips a rope or a tool

games.q: held in the heart — tap the pairs.

s: salok fifty-seven is the last of Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks
the fifty-seventh, on Ang 1429, close to the end of the Granth.
Raam in this salok means only the hero of the Ramayana
across Gurbani, Raam names the one God who pervades everything.
the last salok ends with a warning about death
it ends with what he holds: the Name, which nothing equals.

games.q: after fifty-six saloks about passing, chains and friends who left, the Guru has one line left. what does he say?
o: I have held the Name in my heart; nothing equals it.
games.why: the last word is personal testimony: the one thing the world couldn't take, gripped in the heart.

practice: Choose one short line from the past few weeks that stayed with you, nothing stays, today or tomorrow, rahio, or a single word, like Waheguru, and put a hand on your chest if you like.
Say it silently on each out-breath, gently, like holding a rope without strain, and come back to it when your mind wanders. If you pray, the line can be your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Ur, the heart, the chest. Raam naam ur mai gahio: the Name gripped in the ur, and jaa kai sam nahee koi, nothing equals it.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: ur, the heart or chest; raam naam ur mai gahio, the Name gripped in the heart.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing equals it. What's gripped in the heart can't be taken. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Salok Mahalla 9, salok 57 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429)
